title: Check Bench
context: Grade 4, and this is the topic that stops a wrong answer from travelling. An adult sees an extra sum done after the real one. What is actually being taught is that subtraction carries its own test inside it, worked with different steps: difference plus subtrahend rebuilds the minuend. Reading an answer over again repeats whatever slip produced it, and a child who has only ever read an answer over has no way of finding out that it is wrong.

writeup.why: Find out whether a difference is right without working the same subtraction over again, by putting back what was taken away.
writeup.look: Two bays joined down the middle, the subtraction above and the check below it, with a true and false rail along the foot of the stage.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Check Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the checks written out in full against the workings standing on the bench, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one each time a total is lifted on to the shelf and the second fixed at however many workings this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The two bays stand one above the other on the left of the working area, each 700 by 206, the upper at 64,202 and the lower at 64,430, joined through the 22 tall gap between them by a spine 12 wide running down their middle. The upper bay holds the subtraction on a ruled column mat: headings across the top, the greater number on the upper row, the number taken away under it with the minus sign 40 to its left, a rule 6 tall, and the difference beneath. Drop to check slides copies of the difference and the number taken away down the spine into the lower bay, where they settle stacked with a plus sign to the left of the lower of them and a rule 6 tall under both; the originals never leave the upper bay, so the working being tested is on the stage the whole time the check is being built. The check is added column by column from the ones, each carried one drawn small above the column it goes into, and the total it builds stands under its rule in green. Hold against lifts that total out of the lower bay along a drawn path and stands it on the shelf, 300 by 206 at 826,202, beside a copy of the number the working set out from; the two are read digit for digit from the right, and the match light between them fills only when the last pair agrees and stays dark otherwise, with nothing marked either way and the first column from the right where the two part left ringed in amber. The dice bay is 300 by 206 at 826,430: it rolls five digits, builds a number from them, takes that number away from the largest five digit number and adds the two results back together on the same bench. The verdict rail runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 78 at 64,652, with a true end at its left and a false end at its right; a written statement is dragged to whichever end the check has earned, and a statement the check has failed springs back from the true end with the check still showing and nothing marked. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a difference or a check total is asked for, and on the third phase a pair of verdict keys reading true and false that do the same work as the rail for a child who would rather press than drag. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number standing on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a column that has lent is told by the single strike through its digit and by the smaller value written small above it. Turn it round loads an addition into the upper bay in place of a subtraction, with the plus drawn where the minus stood, and the lower bay then holds a subtraction instead, so that the bench looks the same either way up and the two workings are plainly one another undone.
writeup.finish: The card shows the working the child checked, the check standing under it, and the two totals held side by side.

phases.win: the total lifts, stands beside the number on top and the match light joins them
phases.does: drops the answer and the number taken away into the bay and adds them
phases.goal: difference plus subtrahend lands on the minuend
phases.says: Put back what you took away. Where does it land?
phases.check: You have taken one number away from another and written the answer. Which two numbers do you add to get back to where you started?
phases.feels: putting back what was taken away lands on the number you set out from, every single time
phases.hands: On squared paper work 46,728 - 15,304. Then, underneath it, write the answer with the number that was taken away under it, draw a plus and a rule, and add them. Before the adding starts, ask the child to say which number on the page the total is going to land on, and then cover that number with a finger until the adding is finished.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which number was taken off the bench by the working? Second rung, the phase's: if you put that number back, what should be standing there? Third rung: the bench is cut to a two column subtraction and the child drops the pair and adds it back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the working that produced the answer is the working they know, and running it twice feels like twice the care.
wrong.move: works the subtraction a second time instead of adding anything back, because doing it again is what checking has always meant.
wrong.screen: the second subtraction runs column by column beside the first and lands on exactly the same difference, with every column agreeing. Both runs are left standing side by side, the number the working set out from stays untouched above them, and the shelf stays empty, because nothing has been built that could be stood on it.

wrong.why: the number on top is the one the check is aiming at, and the two largest numbers on the bench look like the pair that belong together.
wrong.move: adds the difference to the number on top instead of to the number that was taken away.
wrong.screen: that addition runs in the lower bay and its total is lifted to the shelf, where it stands plainly taller than the number beside it and the match light stays dark. The three rows in the upper bay are then read out by their names, and the two rows that rebuild the top one light together while the child's pair stays drawn exactly where it was put.

phases.screen: a finished subtraction above an empty check bay
phases.soWhat: Difference plus subtrahend gives the minuend back.
phases.concept: The answer and the number taken away rebuild the start

phases.win: every column of the check is filled and its total is held against the number on top
phases.does: adds the check column by column from the ones and reads the total out
phases.goal: the check is written out in columns rather than glanced at
phases.says: Write the whole check out. Looking at an answer is not checking it.
phases.check: Why is looking at a difference and deciding it seems right not the same thing as checking it?
phases.feels: the check is a sum in its own right and it has to be worked like one
phases.hands: On squared paper work 64,203 - 27,851, then write the check out underneath in full columns, carried ones drawn small above the columns they go into, with nothing done in the head at all. Ask for the check total to be read out place by place before it is compared with anything.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column of the check has been added so far? Second rung, the phase's: which column does a check begin at? Third rung: the check is cut to two columns and the child adds those two and holds the total against the number on top. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the numbers are familiar by now and the working looked tidy while it was being done, and the bench seems to be asking for a judgement rather than for a sum.
wrong.move: looks at the two numbers, says the answer seems about right and gives a verdict without the check bay being touched.
wrong.screen: the check runs anyway at walking pace, column by column from the ones, with each column filling in green as it is added. The child's verdict stays in the answer slot the whole time, and the total the columns build is lifted to the shelf beside the number the working set out from so that the judgement and the check stand together.

wrong.why: the answer the check should reach is already printed on the stage, and the empty squares under the rule look like somewhere to put the number that is wanted.
wrong.move: writes the number from the top of the upper bay into the check's total, because that is what the check is supposed to come to.
wrong.screen: the copied total stays exactly where it was put. The check is then added column by column from the ones with every carried one drawn small above its column, and the total the columns actually build stands beside the copied one with the first column from the right where the two part lit and staying lit.

phases.screen: the check bay open with the columns empty and the plus already drawn
phases.soWhat: Write the check out in full, because glancing at an answer is not checking it.
phases.concept: A check worked all the way through

phases.win: the statement lands on the end the check earned and the true difference stands beside it
phases.does: runs the check, reads the match light and sends the statement to one end
phases.goal: a written statement is judged by the check and not by how it looks
phases.says: Somebody has written this already. Check it before you believe it.
phases.check: Somebody hands you a finished subtraction on a card. What do you do before you agree with it?
phases.feels: a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one until it has been added back
phases.hands: Have each child write a subtraction out neatly on a card and put one digit of the answer wrong on purpose, without saying where. Cards are swapped and each one is judged by adding the answer back, not by looking at it. Whoever finds a wrong card has to say what the answer should have been as well as that it was wrong.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the written answer come to when it is added back on to the number that was taken away? Second rung, the phase's: is that the number the statement started from? Third rung: the statement is cut to a two column one and the child checks it and sends it to an end. The verdict keys stay open.

wrong.why: a statement that has been written out properly looks like a statement somebody has already been through, and a tidy page is hard to doubt.
wrong.move: sends the statement to the true end because it is neatly written and its columns line up.
wrong.screen: the drag springs back from the true end with nothing marked and the statement left where it began. The check then runs of its own accord in the lower bay, adding 52,011 on to 21,340, and its total of 73,351 is lifted to the shelf beside 73,451 with the match light dark and the hundreds column, which is where the two part, left ringed in amber.

wrong.why: a verdict was what the rail asked for, and a wrong answer feels finished the moment it has been called wrong.
wrong.move: sends the statement to the false end and moves on without ever working out what it should have said.
wrong.screen: the statement stays at the false end where the child put it. The working in the upper bay is then opened again column by column from the ones until it builds 52,111, that difference is dropped into the check bay and added on to 21,340, and the total is lifted to the shelf, where it lands on 73,451 and the match light fills.

phases.screen: a statement already written out, with the verdict rail waiting below it
phases.soWhat: Check a written answer before you believe it, and then say what it should have been.
phases.concept: A printed answer can be wrong

phases.win: the other number is left exactly, and the two bays read as one another undone
phases.does: takes one of the two numbers from the total and looks for the other
phases.goal: an addition can be tested by taking one of its numbers away
phases.says: This time it is an addition. How would taking away test it?
phases.check: You have added two numbers together. How could taking away tell you whether the total is right?
phases.feels: the two workings undo each other, so either one can be used to test the other
phases.hands: Write 27,415 + 36,208 on squared paper and add it. Then, without adding anything again, take 36,208 away from the total and see which number is left. Do it once more taking the other number away instead. Finish with the dice game in threes, where a rolled number is taken from 99,999 and the two results are added back together.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the three numbers is the total? Second rung, the phase's: what should be left when one part is taken off the total? Third rung: the bench is cut to a two column addition and the child checks it by taking one number away. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: adding is the working in front of them, and checking has meant doing the same thing again for as long as they have been checking anything.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers together a second time to check the addition.
wrong.screen: the second addition runs beside the first and lands on the same total, column for column and carry for carry, with both runs left standing. The turn it round control then lights on its own, and the lower bay opens with a minus drawn in it and one of the two numbers already waiting underneath the total.

wrong.why: subtraction has always begun from the biggest number on the page, and a total reads as something that was made rather than as a number to work from.
wrong.move: takes the smaller of the two numbers away from the greater one instead of taking either of them away from the total.
wrong.screen: that subtraction runs in the lower bay and leaves 8,793, which is none of the three numbers on the bench, and it is left standing. The three numbers are then named out loud as two parts and a total with the total lit, the check is laid again taking one part away from the total, and both runs stay on the stage together.

phases.screen: an addition handed over in the upper bay with the turn it round control lit
phases.soWhat: To check an addition, take one of its two numbers away from the total and look for the other one.
phases.concept: Addition and subtraction check each other

writeup.delight: The moment hold against is pressed. The total lifts out of the lower bay and travels up the drawn path to the shelf, where it comes to rest beside the number the working set out from. The two are then read off digit for digit from the right, one pair at a time, with each pair lighting as it is read, and the match light between them fills only once the last pair on the left has agreed. Where they part, the reading stops at the first column from the right that parts them, that column keeps a small amber ring, and the light stays dark with nothing else marked anywhere.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a finished subtraction stands in the upper bay with its difference under the rule, and the lower bay is empty with its plus sign already drawn and its columns blank. On the second the two numbers of the check have come down into the lower bay and are stacked with a rule beneath them, every square under that rule still empty. On the third a written statement lies across the middle of the stage, already worked out by somebody else, with the verdict rail waiting along the foot and both of its ends dark. On the fourth an addition sits in the upper bay instead of a subtraction, with the turn it round control lit beside it. The running count at the top left holds the checks written out against the workings on the bench, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the difference under the rule, or the first empty column of the check, or the written statement, or the total of the addition, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what putting back what was taken away would land on. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any subtraction, with the check bay, the verdict rail and the dice bay all open at once. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on adding the answer back, writing the check out in full, judging a written statement, and checking an addition by taking one number away.
voiceLines: Two bays. The working in the upper one, and the putting back in the lower one.
Put back what you took away. Where does it land?
Write the whole check out. Looking at an answer is not checking it.
Somebody has written this already. Check it before you believe it.
This time it is an addition. How would taking away test it?
Another working. Put back what was taken away and see where it lands.
Free play. Any subtraction, the verdict rail live and the dice bay open beside it.
Send them down again and add the whole check out, column by column.
Every check written out in full, and every total held against the number it set out from.

observations.why: Working the same subtraction over again repeats whatever produced the answer the first time.
observations.soWhat: A check that repeats the working is not a check, however carefully it is done.
observations.observe: The check was a different sum from the one it was testing, and that is the only reason it caught anything.

observations.why: Two numbers can only be read against each other properly while both of them are showing.
observations.soWhat: The check and the number it is being tested against belong in the same frame.
observations.observe: The total the check built was stood beside the number the working set out from, not compared from memory.

observations.why: The check adds the whole thing at one go, so it tests the answer and not any single step inside it.
observations.soWhat: A failed check sends you back to the working; it does not hand you the mistake.
observations.observe: When the check failed it said that the working was wrong and never once said which column was wrong.

observations.why: Nothing about the way a number is written down says anything about whether it is true.
observations.soWhat: A printed answer earns belief by being checked, and by nothing else.
observations.observe: A written statement that was wrong looked exactly like one that was right.

source_tool.name: Check Bench
source_tool.blurb: Add the answer back onto the number you took away, and hold the total against the number you started from.

serves.exercise: finding the smaller number from the greater number and the difference between them
checking whether the two given subtraction statements are correct
finding the difference between the given pairs and checking each answer by addition
playing the dice game in threes that takes a number away from the largest five digit number and adds it back

source_tool.description: The stage carries two bays, one above the other, joined down the middle. The upper bay holds the subtraction, set out in columns with the greater number on top. The lower bay is the check: the difference and the subtrahend come down into it, stacked with a plus and a rule under them, and the total that comes out is lifted and held beside the number the working started from, so the two stand together in one frame rather than on two pages. A match light joins them when they read the same and stays dark when they do not, and nothing is marked either way. A verdict rail runs along the foot of the stage with two ends, one reading true and one reading false, and a statement is dragged to whichever end the check has earned. Statements arrive already written out, some of them right and some of them not, and a wrong one cannot be sent to the true end. A turn it round control does the same work the other way: an addition is handed over and one of its two numbers is taken from the total, so subtraction gets to check addition. A dice bay makes a five digit number from rolled digits, takes it from the largest five digit number and adds the two results back together.
source_tool.art_direction: Two bays, the check under the working / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that untie themselves, a rule between the number taken away and the answer, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A subtraction is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the greater number on top, the two numbers aligned by their right ends, the minus sign to the left of the lower row, and a horizontal rule between that row and the answer. A bare line of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach taking away.

A trade is always drawn as both of its halves. The lending column keeps its digit, struck through once, with its new and smaller value written small above it, and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column on its right. A short arrow runs from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right, never the other way.

A check by addition is drawn under the subtraction it tests, and the total it comes to is set beside the number the working started from, so the two can be read against each other without anything being cleared.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, and the answer under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, and a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, so the two halves of one trade are told apart at a glance. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a lending column is told apart by the strike through its digit and by the smaller digit written above it before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Send them down again and add the whole check out, column by column.
voice.onNext: Another working. Put back what was taken away and see where it lands.
voice.opening: Two bays. The working in the upper one, and the putting back in the lower one.
voice.onFinish: Every check written out in full, and every total held against the number it set out from.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any subtraction, the verdict rail live and the dice bay open beside it.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The answer and the number taken away rebuild the start
A check worked all the way through
A printed answer can be wrong
Addition and subtraction check each other

placement.where: After the first long subtraction has been worked and everybody is sure of it. The tool is what keeps the check and the number it is being tested against on the stage together, which paper can only do by being read twice.

answer_key.rule: To check a subtraction, add the difference to the subtrahend. The total has to be the minuend, the number the working started from. If it is not, something in the working is wrong, although the check does not yet say where. The check has to be written out in full, because reading an answer again repeats whatever slip made it. The same tie works the other way: to check an addition, take one of the two numbers away from the total and the other one should be left.
answer_key.wrong: The difference and the subtrahend slide back down into the check bay and are added again column by column, with the total lifted and set beside the number on top so the two can be read together. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Working the columns gives a difference of 32,416.
Add that difference to the subtrahend: 32,416 + 21,543.
The total is 53,959, which is the minuend, so the difference is right.
items.answer: On 53,959, the number the working started from
items.question: Take 21,543 from 53,959, then add your answer back onto 21,543. Where does it land?
items.checkpoint: Difference plus subtrahend gives the minuend back, every time.
items.misconception: Subtracting a second time instead of adding back, which just repeats the same slip.

steps: The ones cannot pay, so a ten comes from the tens column on its left, and 15 - 8 = 7.
Carrying on leftwards gives a difference of 35,167.
The check is written out in columns: 35,167 + 46,208 = 81,375, which is the number on top.
items.question: Subtract 46,208 from 81,375 and write the check out in full.
items.checkpoint: A check is written out in columns, not glanced at.
items.misconception: Saying the answer looks about right and never writing the addition down at all.

steps: Add the written answer back onto the number taken away: 21,242 + 25,140 = 46,382.
That is not 47,382, so the statement does not hold and goes to the false end.
Working the subtraction properly gives 22,242, and 22,242 + 25,140 = 47,382.
items.answer: It is wrong. The true difference is 22,242
items.question: A sheet has 47,382 - 25,140 = 21,242 already written on it. Check it and say whether it holds.
items.checkpoint: A check that does not land on the number on top says the statement is wrong.
items.misconception: Believing a written answer because it is written, and never adding it back.

steps: Take one of the two numbers away from the total: 62,703 - 28,197.
The ones cannot pay and the tens has nothing to give, so the reach goes on to the hundreds, and the working runs leftwards.
What is left is 34,506, which is the other number, so the addition holds.
items.question: A child adds 34,506 and 28,197 and gets 62,703. Use subtraction to check it.
items.checkpoint: Adding and taking away undo each other, so either one can test the other.
items.misconception: Adding the two numbers again to check the addition, which repeats the same steps.

items.question: A difference is 5,214 and the subtrahend is 3,478. What was the number on top?
What do you add to a difference to get back to the number the working started from?
items.final_answer: The subtrahend, which is the number that was taken away

items.question: Subtract 12,304 from 29,857 and check the answer by addition.
The difference between two numbers is 3,946 and the greater number is 8,120. Find the smaller number and check it.
A board reads 63,470 - 41,250 = 22,120. Is the statement right?
items.final_answer: No. The true difference is 22,220, because 22,220 + 41,250 = 63,470

items.question: A board reads 58,916 - 27,504 = 31,412. Is the statement right?
items.final_answer: Yes. Adding 31,412 and 27,504 gives 58,916, the number it started from

items.question: A shopkeeper adds 25,634 and 19,087 and writes 44,721. Check the total by taking one number away.
In a game of three, a rolled number of 12,345 is taken from 99,999 and the answer is written as 87,554. Add it back and say whether it holds.
items.final_answer: It is wrong. Adding 87,554 and 12,345 gives 99,899, not 99,999, so the difference should be 87,654

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the subtraction, set out in columns
sends the difference and the subtrahend down into the lower bay
adds the two in the lower bay and lifts the total
stands the total beside the number the working started from
joins the two when they read the same and stays dark when they do not
takes a written statement to the true end or the false end
hands over an addition and checks it by taking one number away

teaching_notes: The chapter's own worked check is the one to read aloud before anything is opened: taking 56,986 from 98,975 leaves 41,989, and putting 41,989 back onto 56,986 rebuilds 98,975. Say it as putting back what was taken away, not as a second sum, because that is the whole reason it catches anything. Insist that the check is written out in columns. A child who reads the answer over again will repeat the same slip and feel surer afterwards than before. The verdict rail is worth the slowest work: hand over statements that are already written out, some right and some not, and let the class discover that a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one until it is tested. When a statement fails, stop and ask what the check does and does not tell them. It says the working is wrong; it does not say which column. Finish on the turn it round control, so that addition and subtraction are held as one another undone rather than as two separate chapters. The dice game at the end of the chapter is this whole topic as a race, and it works best with the roles swapped every round.
generation_prompt: Build a checking tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, split into two bays one above the other and joined down the middle. The upper bay holds a subtraction on a ruled column mat, greater number on top, minus sign to the left of the lower row, a rule between that row and the answer. A drop to check control slides the difference and the subtrahend down into the lower bay, where they stack with a plus and a rule and are added column by column from the ones with carries drawn small above their columns. The total is then lifted and stood beside the original number on top, inside the same frame, and a match light joins the two when they read the same and stays dark when they do not, with nothing marked either way. A verdict rail runs along the foot of the stage with a true end and a false end, taking a written statement dragged to whichever end the check has earned; a wrong statement cannot be dropped at the true end and the drag springs back with the check still showing. A turn it round control loads an addition into the upper bay instead and tests it by taking one of its two numbers from the total. A dice bay rolls five digits, forms a number from them, takes it from the largest five digit number and adds the two results back together. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Work the subtraction in the upper bay. Then drop your answer and the number you took away into the bay below. Add them and hold the total against the number you started from. If the two match, the working is right. If they do not, go back and work it again.
